newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African business criticises new labour bill.
newsitem.headline: S.African business criticises new labour bill.

text.p: South African organised business said on Friday it feared a new employment bill approved by the cabinet this week would increase labour costs.
The South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) criticised the bill's provisions which would increase the overtime rate and leave allocations.
Annual, sick and maternity leave entitlements would be increased and the bill proposes the introduction of "family responsibility" leave.
"These increased benefits represent additional costs to the individual business enterprise and will add to overall unit labour costs," Sacob president Philip Krawitz said in a statement.
But the chamber said it welcomed the absence of a statutory imposed goal of a 40-hour work week.
Labour Minister Tito Mboweni released the bill on Thursday, and it now goes to the National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) for further discussions.
In line with policy plans released in February last year, the bill retains proposals to reduce weekly working hours to 45 from 46 hours for all workers, including mine, farm and shift workers.
Business South Africa chairman Hans Smith said business was still worried the decrease in working hours and increased leave would raise unit labour costs.
"The question business will be asking in the (Nedlac) negotiations is how rising labour standards can be balanced with the urgent imperatives of growth and creation of more jobs," he said.

The country's largest labour federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions was scheduled to announce later on Friday if it would go ahead with a national strike on May 12 over the employment bill.
Labour is concerned that proposals designed to protect workers will be watered down.
Proposals in the bill, which for the first time also included public service workers, do not meet Cosatu's demand for phasing in a 40-hour working week.
